3.text: the territories, he stepped over to Rɪˊnto, caught him by the head, and lifted

4.text: him from the ground up in the air. Then he put him down. “Now, say,

5.text: what do you want?” he asked with a smile. His temper was quite sweet and

6.text: peaceful, and he did not want to hurt anybody. Rɪˊnto said nothing, and

7.text: went away to his own house. The next day he came into the fortress, and

8.text: brought with him expiatory presents, — a reindeer-tongue for my friend, as

9.text: being the stronger of us two; and a piece of ordinary meat for me. “I was

10.text: ugly yesterday,” said he. “Take this kɪˊtkau,¹ as is the custom; and now

11.text: give me my draught of alcohol.” This was so ingenuous, that my friend was

12.text: quite charmed, and insisted on having Rɪˊnto’s wish gratified.

13.text: THEFT. — As I have stated before, thefts frequently occur among the

14.text: Chukchee, especially among the reindeer-breeders. The chief objects taken

15.text: are reindeer. Retribution for theft is of the same nature as that for more

16.text: serious crimes, — either wrestling-matches and personal chastisement, or the

17.text: payment of damages and a fine. I was told that the common rule required

18.text: that the amount paid shall equal the value of the stolen article, together with

19.text: a certain surplus as a fine for the deed. This, however, may happen when

20.text: the thief confesses his action and expresses a desire to make it good. —

21.text: “compelled by shame,” as the Chukchee say. If the thief persists in denying

22.text: his guilt, however, it is difficult to make him return the stolen property.

23.text: Thus the result depends much on the strength and the temper of the con-

24.text: testing parties. I will mention a few such cases within my knowledge.

25.text: One reindeer-breeder, a man of peaceful temper, lost a group of reindeer,

26.text: nine in number, which strayed away from the herd, as reindeer often do, and

27.text: could not be found. It appeared afterwards that they had gone to the herd

28.text: of one of the neighboring camps, and had been appropriated by the master.

29.text: His own camp assistant gave information of the fact; but the offender was

30.text: obstinate, and denied it till the end. Then the wronged man became angry,

31.text: and sent his people to seek retribution. His son and one of his neighbors

32.text: visited the herd of the offender in the latter’s absence, and took from it two

33.text: strong driving-reindeer, one young buck well broken, and three reindeer of

34.text: the average sort. They said to the herdsmen, “Go and tell the master that

35.text: we did this.” Still this was not enough. The next day they visited the camp

36.text: of the unfortunate thief. The nephew was of a quarrelsome disposition, and

37.text: said before departing, “Maybe he will show his anger. Then we will give

38.text: him a thrashing.” They came to the camp, and spent some time there talk-

39.text: ing with the house-mates of the offender. He, however, sat quite silent and

40.text: looked at the ground. He had not the courage to pick a quarrel. I should

41.text: also mention that the quarrelsome nephew belonged to a strong family, and
